subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 17 periods = 680 minutes
Total: 17 periods · 11h 20min

periods.textbook_anchor: A Potter's Family — Discussing what pots are used for and what other things potters make (p. 137)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of pots, gullak, kulhad, and birdbath on p. 137

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to look at the opening illustration of Mini and Appooppan on Textbook p. 137. Ask: 'What do you see here? Who might these people be? What are they making?' Allow two or three students to share freely.

Read aloud the story of Mini and Appooppan together, pausing at natural breaks. Students identify each family member's role: Appooppan wets and kneads clay, shapes it on the stone wheel; Ammu manages the kiln; Mini decorates with patterns and colours. Teacher writes each role on the board as students name it.

Open discussion using Textbook p. 137: 'What are pots used for?' Students share uses they know — storing water, cooking, drinking, saving coins. Teacher adds the textbook examples (pots, gullak, kulhad, birdbath) to the board list only if not already mentioned.

Second discussion: 'What other kinds of things do potters make?' Students contribute examples from their own experience — flower pots, diyas, toys, tiles. Teacher gently prompts: 'Has anyone seen a potter at work near your home or at a fair?' to draw out local knowledge.
Closing: each student says one thing the potter's family does together. Teacher summarises: clay from the earth becomes useful objects through the family's shared work.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the roles different family members play in a traditional craft process.
periods.section_context: Mini, Appooppan, Ammu, clay-kneading, stone wheel, kiln firing, decoration with patterns and colours, pots, gullak, kulhad, birdbath.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether anyone in their own family or neighbourhood makes things by hand — pottery, baskets, brooms — to naturally draw out the idea that craft knowledge lives in families and communities across generations.

periods.activity_title: Why Bake the Pot? Exploring the Kiln
periods.textbook_anchor: A Potter's Family — Investigating why the pot is baked in a kiln (p. 137)
materials: Two small lumps of clay or dough — one sun-dried, one unbaked raw
Tray or newspaper to protect desks
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of the kiln on p. 137

time_bands.activity: Teacher places two lumps of clay or dough on each group's tray: one that has been left to air-dry overnight and one fresh, soft lump. Ask: 'Feel both. What do you notice? Are they the same or different?'

Students in pairs press, poke, and gently try to shape each lump, then drip a few drops of water onto each. They observe: which one holds water? Which one crumbles or softens? Teacher circulates, asking 'What is happening? Why might this matter for a pot you want to carry water in?'

Discussion anchored to Textbook p. 137: 'Why is the pot baked in a kiln?' Students connect their hands-on finding — the dry lump is harder, resists water — to the idea that baking drives out moisture and makes clay strong and long-lasting. Teacher writes key words on the board: wet clay → shape → kiln → hard pot.
Students draw a simple four-step sequence in their notebooks: (1) wet clay, (2) shaped pot, (3) kiln, (4) finished pot. They label each step with one word.
Quick share: two or three students hold up their sequence drawings. Class agrees on the order together. Teacher names the transformation: heat changes soft clay into something that lasts.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain why a process step (applying heat) changes a material's properties, using evidence from a hands-on comparison.
periods.section_context: Wet clay vs. air-dried clay, water-resistance test, kiln baking, four-step pot-making sequence.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students mention other things baked by heat — bread, bricks, earthen lamps — welcome these connections; ask what is common in each case to draw out the idea that heat hardens or transforms materials.

periods.textbook_anchor: A Potter's Family — Making clay from collected soil and shaping two objects (p. 138)
materials: Soil collected from a damp patch in the school garden (teacher pre-collected)
Fine mesh sieve or muslin cloth

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the activity steps aloud from Textbook p. 138. Students read along. Teacher shows the pre-collected soil and the sieve, asking: 'What might be mixed into this soil that we don't want in our clay?'

Small groups sieve the soil over a tray, removing pebbles, leaves, and grit. They add water gradually, mixing and kneading until the mixture becomes dough-like — not too sticky, not crumbly. Teacher moves between groups: 'How does it feel now compared to when it was dry?'

Each student shapes two small objects of their choice — a pinch pot, a tiny animal, a flat tile, a bead — from their prepared clay. Objects are placed on a labelled newspaper square to dry in the sun or on a windowsill. Students observe the texture and weight of the fresh clay object.

Students write two sentences in their notebooks: (1) what they made, and (2) one thing they noticed about the clay while working with it (sticky, smooth, heavy, cool). Teacher asks: 'What do you think will happen to your object as it dries?'
Closing: teacher highlights that this is exactly how potters begin — soil + water + kneading — and that this knowledge has been passed down in families for thousands of years.

periods.implied_lo: Students can follow a multi-step process to prepare a natural material and shape it into a simple object.
periods.section_context: Soil collection, sieving, water-mixing, kneading into clay dough, shaping two objects, sun-drying.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to notice that the clay-making steps mirror what Appooppan does at the start of pot-making — wetting and kneading — to reinforce that they are practising an ancient craft process, not just a classroom activity.

periods.textbook_anchor: A Potter's Family — Drawing products seen at the potter's place in the activity box (p. 137)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of gullak, kulhad, birdbath, and decorated pots on p. 137

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the textbook illustrations on Textbook p. 137 with the class, naming each object aloud: pot for water, gullak, kulhad, birdbath. Ask students: 'Have you seen any of these at home, at a shop, or at a fair? What else do you think potters make?'

Students draw at least three products that a potter makes in the activity box on Textbook p. 137 or on drawing paper. They add colour and, if they wish, a small decorative pattern on each object — inspired by Mini's decoration work. Teacher circulates, prompting: 'What shape is the bottom? Is the neck wide or narrow?'

Gallery walk: students place their drawings on their desks and do a quiet walk around to see classmates' work. Each student chooses one drawing that shows something they had not drawn themselves and remembers it.

Closing discussion: 'Which object in your drawing do you think would be hardest to make? Why?' Two or three students share. Teacher notes that each object requires skill built over years — craft knowledge lives in the family and the community.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present observations about craft objects through drawing, capturing shape and surface detail.
periods.section_context: Potter's products: pots, gullak, kulhad, birdbath; decorative patterns; gallery walk of drawn objects.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students mention diyas, tiles, or toys not shown in the textbook, celebrate these additions — they reflect real regional variety in what potters make, and this regional diversity is worth naming for the class.

periods.activity_title: Patterns in the World Around Us
periods.textbook_anchor: Patterns in Nature — Looking around for patterns on plants and drawing a leaf pattern (p. 140)
materials: A few leaves brought from the school garden (teacher pre-collected — fresh leaves of two or three different plants)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of zebra stripes, leopard spots, squirrel stripes, and neem leaf arrangement on p. 140

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds up the pre-collected leaves one at a time. Students observe quietly, then share: 'What do you notice on the surface of this leaf?' Teacher introduces the word 'pattern' — a repeating shape or colour — and points to the veins, the serrated edge, the overall outline as examples.

Students open Textbook p. 140 and study the nature photographs. Teacher asks: 'Point to a pattern on the zebra. Point to a pattern on the leopard. Point to a pattern on the squirrel.' Students identify each and describe it in one word: stripes, spots, lines. Class discusses: 'Where else in nature might we find patterns?'

Observation and drawing: students choose one of the pre-collected leaves or look at the neem-leaf illustration on Textbook p. 140. They observe carefully and draw the leaf's pattern in the box provided on Textbook p. 140, adding as much detail as they can — veins, edge shape, tip.
Students write one sentence below their drawing: 'The pattern I can see on this leaf is ___.' Teacher asks two or three students to share and describe their pattern in their own words.
Closing question: 'Why do you think so many living things have patterns?' Accept all answers — camouflage, beauty, recognition — without closing off the question.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record repeating patterns on natural objects through careful looking and drawing.
periods.section_context: Zebra stripes, leopard spots, squirrel stripes, neem leaf arrangement, leaf vein patterns, plant leaf observation and drawing.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether any student has noticed patterns on plants or animals near their home — a striped caterpillar, a spotted mushroom, the rings of a tree stump — to connect the textbook examples to the immediate local environment.

periods.textbook_anchor: Patterns in Nature — Drawing an animal with body patterns and a pattern found on things (p. 140)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook photographs of patterned animals and patterned pottery on p. 140

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly revisits the textbook photographs on Textbook p. 140 — patterned animals and patterned pottery. Ask: 'When artists decorate a pot, where do you think they get their ideas?' Allow students to speculate freely before reading the textbook explanation that artists draw inspiration from plants and animals.

Drawing task 1 — Animals: students draw an animal of their choice that has a pattern on its body (Textbook p. 140). They then add the pattern carefully, trying to make it look like the real animal. Teacher circulates, asking: 'Is your pattern repeating? How many times does it repeat?'

Drawing task 2 — Things: students draw a pattern they have noticed on an object at home, in school, or in the street — a tile floor, a woven mat, a printed cloth, a fence, pottery (Textbook p. 140). They fill the box with that repeating pattern.
Pair share: each student shows both drawings to a partner and says which pattern they liked drawing more and why. Teacher listens for the link between nature patterns and human-made patterns.

Closing: teacher draws one student's animal pattern and one student's object pattern on the board side by side, pointing out that human makers often copy nature's designs — a tradition as old as pottery itself.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent patterns observed in nature and in human-made objects through drawing, identifying the repeating element.
periods.section_context: Patterned animal drawing, patterned object drawing, nature-to-art inspiration connection, regional pottery decoration traditions.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students mention rangoli, kantha embroidery, block-print fabric, or painted pottery from their home region, invite them to describe the patterns — these are living examples of artists taking inspiration from nature, exactly as the textbook describes.

periods.textbook_anchor: Patterns in Nature — Arranging images of the pot-making process in correct order by numbering 1 to 6 (p. 139)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook sequence images of pot-making stages on p. 139

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 139 and study the six images silently for a moment. Teacher asks: 'Without writing anything yet — what do you think is happening in each picture? Tell your neighbour.' Brief pair talk follows.

Students individually number the images from 1 to 6, placing them in the order they think the process happens. Teacher circulates without correcting yet, noting where disagreements occur to use in discussion.

Whole-class discussion: teacher calls on different students for each step. Where there is disagreement, ask the class: 'Can you bake a pot before you shape it? Can you shape it before the clay is ready?' Students reason through the order using cause and effect.

Once the class agrees on the correct sequence, students check their own numbering and correct if needed. Teacher asks: 'Which step do you think takes the longest? Which needs the most skill?' A brief open discussion follows.
Closing: teacher connects the sequence to the idea that craft has an order — each step depends on the one before it, and that knowledge is what makes a skilled potter.

periods.implied_lo: Students can sequence the stages of a making process in logical order, justifying each step using cause-and-effect reasoning.
periods.section_context: Six-image pot-making sequence: clay collection, wetting and kneading, shaping on wheel, surface decoration, kiln loading, finished pot.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Use students' disagreements productively — if two orderings are proposed, ask both students to explain their reasoning before the class decides, modelling that evidence and logic, not volume, settle sequencing questions.

periods.textbook_anchor: Brick by Brick — Discussing whether all houses are made of bricks and what other materials are used (p. 144)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of brick-making and mud houses on p. 144

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 144 and reads the story of Rohan watching bricks being laid in Jaipur. Ask: 'Has anyone watched a building being built? What did you see the workers doing?' Students share observations freely.

Teacher draws a simple two-column table on the board: POTTERY | BRICKS. Together the class fills it in: both start with clay/mud, both are shaped, both go into a kiln to harden. Teacher: 'What do you notice? Are these processes really so different?'

Discussion using Textbook p. 144: 'Are all houses made of bricks?' Students contribute — stone houses, mud houses, bamboo homes, tents, houseboats. Teacher writes materials on the board: mud, stone, wood, bamboo, brick, canvas. 'Why might people use different materials?'

Second discussion: 'What do you think are other materials used to build houses?' The textbook passage on mud houses and cow-dung plaster is read aloud. Students discuss why mud is good — it keeps homes cool, it is local, it is cheap. Teacher asks: 'What does the environment around a house have to do with what it is built from?'
Students write two or three sentences in their notebooks about the houses in their own neighbourhood — what materials are used — drawing on the textbook question on Textbook p. 144.

periods.implied_lo: Students can compare two making processes to identify shared steps, and connect the materials used for shelter to the local environment.
periods.section_context: Brick-making from mud moulds, kiln baking, Rohan and the building site, mud houses with cow-dung plaster, building materials (mud, stone, wood, bamboo, brick, canvas).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether any of them have seen or lived in a mud house, or know of one nearby — this grounds the textbook passage in lived experience and opens space for students from diverse housing backgrounds to contribute as experts.

periods.textbook_anchor: Brick by Brick — Writing about why mud houses are better for the environment (p. 144)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of a traditional mud house on p. 144

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads the mud-house passage from Textbook p. 144 aloud, slowly. Students listen with their books open. After reading, teacher asks: 'What did you hear that surprised you? What did you already know?'

Think-pair-share: 'Why do you think mud houses are better for the environment?' Students think silently, then talk with a partner. Pairs share one idea each; teacher writes key ideas on the board: made from local soil, no factory needed, cow-dung plaster is natural, keeps cool without electricity, biodegrades safely.

Students write their own response to the textbook question on Textbook p. 144 in their notebooks — at least two reasons — in their own words. Teacher circulates, asking: 'Is that a reason about nature, about cost, or about the people who live there?'

Reflection: 'Are there any problems with a mud house? What might happen in heavy rain?' Students think through trade-offs. Teacher does not resolve the tension — the aim is careful thinking, not a single correct answer.

Closing: teacher names the value being explored — choosing materials that are kind to the earth — and asks students to carry that question home: 'What is one material in your house that comes directly from nature?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can give reasoned explanations for why a traditional building practice is environmentally suited to its context.
periods.section_context: Mud houses, cow-dung plaster as natural insect repellent and coolant, local soil as building material, environmental reasoning, trade-offs in house construction.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to think about who builds mud houses and where — farmers, people in warm dry regions — to connect shelter choices to geography and livelihood without presenting mud houses as inferior to brick buildings.

periods.textbook_anchor: Brick by Brick — Looking at pictures and guessing the name of each type of house to fill in the table (p. 145)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook pictures of tent, multi-storey building, stone house, and houseboat on p. 145

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 145 and look at the pictures quietly. Teacher asks: 'Can you guess where in India — or the world — each of these houses might be found? What clues in the picture help you decide?'

Students study each picture carefully and fill in the table on Textbook p. 145: name of the house type and what it is made of. Teacher circulates; where students are unsure, prompt: 'Look at the walls — are they wood, fabric, stone, or brick? Look at the roof shape — why might it be that shape?'

Whole-class comparison: teacher draws a four-row table on the board matching the textbook. Students contribute their answers row by row. Where different students gave different names (e.g. 'tent' vs. 'nomad's home'), explore why both can be correct. Teacher adds: 'What kind of weather or place would make this house a good idea?'
Students write one sentence for each house type in their notebooks explaining why it suits its environment: 'A houseboat suits people who live on water because…'
Closing question: 'If you could live in any of these houses for one week, which would you choose? Why?' Two or three students share, giving a reason.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify different types of shelter from visual observation and match each to the environmental or geographic context it suits.
periods.section_context: Tent, multi-storey building, stone house, houseboat; table of house types and materials; environment-to-shelter matching.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If a student mentions a house type not in the textbook — a thatched roof house, an igloo, a stilt house — welcome it and ask what problem that design solves, extending the observation into reasoning.

periods.activity_title: Make a Mini Wall — Test Two Arrangements
periods.textbook_anchor: Brick by Brick — Making bricks and stacking them in two arrangements to test which is sturdier (p. 146)
materials: Atta (dough) or soft clay — pre-prepared by teacher
Empty matchboxes or small paper boxes as moulds
periods.visual_aids: Textbook diagram showing two brick-stacking arrangements on p. 146

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows the two stacking diagrams on Textbook p. 146 and asks: 'What is different about the way the bricks are arranged in each picture?' Students describe: in one the bricks are aligned in straight columns; in the other they are staggered. Teacher poses the question: 'Which do you think will be sturdier? Make a prediction.'

Groups of three press small portions of dough or clay into matchbox moulds to make eight to ten uniform 'bricks'. They then build two short walls side by side on their tray — one with aligned joints, one with staggered joints — following the diagrams on Textbook p. 146.

Groups gently push each wall from the side with one finger, observing which holds together and which collapses more easily. Students record in their notebooks: wall type → what happened when pushed. Teacher asks: 'Why do you think the staggered arrangement holds better?'

Groups share findings. Teacher builds understanding: staggered joints distribute force across more bricks — real builders use this principle for the same reason. Ask: 'Where have you seen this pattern in real buildings or in everyday objects like floor tiles?'

Closing: teacher connects the activity to the broader chapter — clay shaped into bricks, arranged by skilled workers, builds the houses the class has been discussing. Making things requires both material knowledge and structural thinking.

periods.implied_lo: Students can carry out a fair comparison test, record what they observe, and use the evidence to explain why one structural arrangement is stronger than another.
periods.section_context: Dough or clay bricks, matchbox moulds, aligned joint arrangement, staggered joint arrangement, push test, structural stability comparison.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage students to articulate their prediction before building, so they can compare it with their result — this is the core of inquiry: what I expected vs. what I found, and why the difference matters.

periods.activity_title: Safety at the Site — Safety at Home and School
periods.textbook_anchor: Brick by Brick — Discussing safety rules at home and at school (p. 146)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of construction-site workers wearing safety gear on p. 146

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 146 and draws attention to the image of workers at a construction site — helmets, boots, and other protective gear. Ask: 'Why do you think these workers are wearing helmets? What could happen if they did not?'

Discussion: 'Are there any safety rules at home?' Students share rules they know — don't touch the stove, don't go near the roof edge, don't play with electrical sockets, hold the stair rail. Teacher writes them on the board under HOME.

Second discussion: 'Do you have any safety rules at school?' Students name rules — walk, don't run in corridors; don't climb the window; wash hands before eating. Teacher writes under SCHOOL. Ask: 'Why do you think these rules exist? Who gets hurt if we don't follow them?'

Students choose one safety rule from either list and draw a small poster in their notebooks showing the rule in action — a person doing the safe thing — with a one-sentence caption. No external materials needed; pencil drawing is enough.
Closing: three or four students share their poster. Teacher names the value: safety rules protect everyone — workers, family members, classmates. Rules are a way of caring for the people around us.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify safety practices in different settings and explain the reasoning behind each rule.
periods.section_context: Construction-site safety gear (helmets, boots), home safety rules, school safety rules, poster drawing of one safety rule.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students raise a safety concern that is genuinely local — a broken step, an open drain near school — treat it seriously and acknowledge that noticing hazards is the first step in keeping a community safe.

periods.activity_title: Writing What We Know — Pot-Making and Kilns
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Writing about the process of pot-making and what a kiln is (p. 147)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the two writing prompts from Textbook p. 147 aloud: 'What is the process of pot-making?' and 'What is a kiln?' Students think silently for a moment, then briefly tell a partner what they remember without looking at notes.

Students write their response to the first prompt — the process of pot-making — in their own words, in at least three steps. Teacher circulates, asking individuals: 'What comes after shaping? What does heat do to the clay?' without giving the answer.

Students write their response to the second prompt — what a kiln is — in two or three sentences. They should explain not just what it is but why it is used. Teacher checks that students include the function, not just the name.

Pair check: partners swap notebooks and read each other's answers. Each writer gets one piece of feedback from their partner: 'You explained the kiln well' or 'I think you missed one step in the process.' Students may add one sentence if they wish.

Closing: teacher notes that being able to write a process in order — step by step — is a skill used by scientists, engineers, and craft-makers alike. The words belong to the student, not just to the textbook.

periods.implied_lo: Students can write a sequenced account of a making process and explain the purpose of a key step, using their own words.
periods.section_context: Pot-making process in written steps, kiln definition and function, peer feedback on written responses.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage students to use the sequence words they know — first, then, after that, finally — to give their writing a clear order; this is a literacy-science crossover that supports both subjects.

periods.activity_title: Where Do Artists Get Their Ideas?
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Writing about how artists get ideas for their art (p. 147)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook photographs of patterned Indian pottery from different regions (p. 140, cross-reference for visual support)

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the discussion prompt from Textbook p. 147: 'How do artists get ideas for their arts?' Students respond freely. Teacher accepts all ideas — dreams, feelings, looking at things around them — without evaluating them yet.

Teacher steers the discussion to the chapter's key idea: artists observe nature — stripes, spots, leaf shapes, flower forms — and use those patterns in their decorations. Ask: 'Can you think of a pattern from nature that you have seen on something made by a person — a cloth, a pot, a wall?' Students share examples.

Students write two or three sentences in their notebooks responding to the prompt on Textbook p. 147. Teacher asks them to include at least one example from nature and one example of something made by a person that uses that pattern.

'What would happen if there were no patterns in nature?' Students discuss in pairs, then share with the class. Teacher draws out ideas: animals might not be able to hide, flowers might not attract pollinators, art might look very different. Accept all reasoning.
Closing: teacher reflects that the same act of careful observation that makes a good scientist also makes a good artist — both look closely at the world before they work.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect observation of natural patterns to artistic inspiration, and discuss what the world might look like if patterns were absent.
periods.section_context: Artists' sources of inspiration, nature patterns translated into art, 'what if no patterns in nature' reasoning, regional pottery decoration.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students mention a specific regional art form — Warli painting, Madhubani, Gond art, Kolam — invite them to describe the patterns used; these are living traditions where artists have always drawn from nature, and the connection to this chapter is direct.

periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Drawing and colouring any three different kinds of houses (p. 147)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook pictures of diverse house types on p. 145 (available for reference)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reminds the class of the variety of houses discussed and observed across the chapter — mud houses, tents, houseboats, stone houses, multi-storey buildings. Students choose three kinds they want to draw. They may use Textbook p. 145 as a visual reference.

Students draw and colour three different kinds of houses on Textbook p. 147 or on drawing paper. Under each drawing they write the name of the house type and one material it is made from. Teacher circulates, prompting: 'What does the roof look like? What colour would the walls be?'

Students add one sentence to each drawing: 'This house is good for ___ because ___.' This connects the creative task to the reasoning from earlier in the chapter about why different environments call for different shelters.

Small group share: groups of four show each other their drawings and read their sentences aloud. The group identifies which three house types appear across all their drawings and which one was drawn by the most people.
Closing: teacher names the value of housing diversity — there is no single best house; the right shelter depends on the land, the weather, the materials available, and the way people live.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent diverse shelter types through drawing and label each with its material and the environmental reason for its design.
periods.section_context: Three house types drawn and coloured, labels of house name and building material, one-sentence environment-to-shelter reasoning per house.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Accept drawings of house types the textbook did not show — thatched roof houses, stilt houses, cave dwellings — if a student can name the material and give a reason; the goal is environment-to-shelter reasoning, not reproduction of textbook images.

periods.activity_title: How Are Everyday Objects Made? — A Class Inquiry
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Finding out how commonly used objects like pencils, erasers, pens, and notebooks are made (p. 147)
materials: A pencil, an eraser, a pen, and a notebook — one of each on the teacher's desk

time_bands.activity: Teacher places the pencil, eraser, pen, and notebook on the desk. 'You use each of these every day. But do you know what they are made from? Where do the materials come from?' Students share initial ideas freely — wood, rubber, plastic, paper.

Small groups each take one object. Using what they already know — from the chapter's clay and brick material discussions, from observations, and from what elders have told them — they reason through: What material is it made of? Where might that material come from? How might it be shaped? They note their ideas.

Groups report back one at a time. Teacher writes each object's proposed material chain on the board: pencil → wood (tree) + graphite (mined) → shaped and baked; eraser → rubber (rubber tree) → moulded; notebook → paper (wood pulp). The class discusses: 'Which of these involves a material from nature being changed by heat or pressure — like clay becoming a pot?'

Students write in their notebooks: for one object of their choice — pencil, eraser, pen, or notebook — they write the steps of making it as they understand them now, noting where they are unsure. Teacher: 'It is fine to write "I think…" or "I am not sure about this step."'

Closing: teacher reads the textbook prompt on Textbook p. 147 — asking elders how everyday objects are made — and invites students to ask one elder at home about one object this week. The inquiry continues beyond this classroom.

periods.implied_lo: Students can trace the material origins of an everyday object and describe the sequence of steps by which a natural material is transformed into it.
periods.section_context: Pencil, eraser, pen, notebook — materials and making processes; nature-to-object transformation chains; reasoning under uncertainty.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If a student knows from an elder how something is made — charcoal pencils, handmade paper, natural rubber — invite them to share; this is exactly the kind of knowledge the chapter honours: learning from people who make things.

periods.activity_title: Making Things — Bringing the Chapter Together
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Discussing why we have different kinds of houses and what would happen if there were no patterns in nature (p. 147)
materials: Notebooks and pencils for final reflection writing
periods.visual_aids: Chalkboard concept web drawn during the unit

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a large web on the board with 'Making Things' at the centre and four spokes: CLAY, PATTERNS, BRICKS AND HOUSES, MATERIALS WE USE. Ask: 'What do you remember from this chapter that belongs on each spoke?' Students call out ideas; teacher adds them to the web.

Discussion thread 1 — 'Why do we have different kinds of houses?' Students discuss in pairs, then share with the class. Teacher builds the answer on the board: geography, climate, available materials, way of life. Ask: 'What does this tell us about the relationship between people and the environment they live in?'

Discussion thread 2 — 'What would happen if there were no patterns in nature?' Students revisit this question from Textbook p. 147 with the full chapter behind them now. Connect patterns in nature → artists observe → decorate pottery → culture is shaped by the natural world. Ask: 'So patterns in nature are not just beautiful — they do what else?'

Individual reflection writing: students choose one of these prompts and write four to five sentences — (a) 'The most interesting making process I learned about is ___ because…', or (b) 'Nature and human making are connected because…' This is their own synthesis, in their own voice.

Closing circle: each student says one word that sums up what this chapter is about for them. Teacher ends: across pottery, patterns, bricks, and everyday objects, the chapter shows one thing — people look at the natural world around them and use it to make the things they need.

assessment_items.question_text: In Mini's family, Appooppan wets and kneads the clay, Ammu manages the kiln, and Mini decorates the pots. What does this tell us about traditional craft work?

options.label: A
options.text: Decoration is done first, before the clay is shaped on the wheel.

options.label: B
options.text: Different family members share different roles to make the craft work.

options.label: C
options.text: Only one person in a family can learn a craft skill.

options.label: D
options.text: The kiln is the most important part, so Ammu does the most skilled job.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. This item checks whether students grasped the cooperative family structure of craft production, not just individual facts about each person.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the roles different family members play in a traditional craft process.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student missed the central message of shared craft roles and holds a misconception that craft skill is exclusive to one person.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Shows the student ranked roles by perceived importance rather than understanding cooperative interdependence — a common error when one role sounds more dramatic.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a misunderstanding of the pot-making sequence: decoration happens after shaping and firing, not before.

assessment_items.question_text: A student tested two lumps of clay — one fresh and soft, one left to dry. She dripped water on both. The fresh lump absorbed water quickly and became soggy. The dry lump resisted the water and stayed hard. Why do potters bake their pots in a kiln instead of just leaving them to air-dry?
expected_elements: Baking drives out moisture more completely than air-drying alone.
The kiln's heat makes the clay permanently hard and water-resistant.
A pot that is only air-dried will soften or break when it holds water or liquids.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for any response that links kiln heat to permanent hardening and water-resistance. Award partial credit if the student states the kiln makes the pot hard but does not connect this to water-resistance.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain why a process step (applying heat) changes a material's properties, using evidence from a hands-on comparison.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Baking drives out moisture more completely than air-drying alone.
The kiln's heat makes the clay permanently hard and water-resistant.
A pot that is only air-dried will soften or break when it holds water or liquids.

assessment_items.question_text: A student collected damp soil from the school garden, sieved out pebbles and leaves, added water, and kneaded it until it was soft enough to shape. She then made a small pinch pot and left it in the sun. List the steps she followed in the correct order, and name one thing she would need to check before she started shaping.
expected_elements: Steps in order: collect damp soil → sieve to remove pebbles, leaves, grit → add water → knead until dough-like → shape the object → leave in sun to dry.
Before shaping, she should check that the clay is neither too sticky nor too crumbly — it should hold together when pressed into a ball.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for correct sequence (allow minor reordering of water-add and knead if student explains them together) plus a sensible pre-shaping check. Award partial credit for correct sequence without the check, or vice versa.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can follow a multi-step process to prepare a natural material and shape it into a simple object.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

expected_elements: Steps in order: collect damp soil → sieve to remove pebbles, leaves, grit → add water → knead until dough-like → shape the object → leave in sun to dry.
Before shaping, she should check that the clay is neither too sticky nor too crumbly — it should hold together when pressed into a ball.

assessment_items.task: Draw two or three things that a potter makes. For each object you draw, add one decorative pattern on its surface — a pattern you have seen on a pot, a leaf, an animal, or a piece of cloth. Write the name of each object below its drawing.
assessment_items.scaffold: Choose objects with different shapes — for example, a tall pot, a round piggy bank, a small cup. Look at the surface of each object: is it smooth all over, or does it have bumps, ridges, or painted lines? Add a pattern that repeats — stripes, dots, leaf shapes, or wavy lines.
format_of_output: Pencil or colour-pencil drawings of two or three potter's products
A repeating decorative pattern on the surface of each object
The name of each object written beneath its drawing
assessment_items.annotation: Credit any recognisable pottery object (pot, cup, piggy bank, birdbath, diya, flower pot, toy). Credit any pattern that repeats — it need not be complex. The object name may be in any language the student is comfortable with.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present observations about craft objects through drawing, capturing shape and surface detail.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can translate observations of real craft objects into a visual representation that captures both form (shape) and surface decoration (pattern).
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold steers students toward objects with different shapes and toward patterns that repeat — look for evidence that the student chose intentionally rather than drawing random marks.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: distinct object shapes, clearly repeating patterns, labelled correctly. Weak: objects that look identical, random scribbles rather than repeating patterns, no labels.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may describe their pattern in words alongside a simple outline shape. Students who excel may add colour and more complex pattern variations.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing is the primary mode used in the textbook activity and the most natural way for Grade III students to record observations of three-dimensional craft objects.

assessment_items.question_text: A student looked carefully at a neem leaf and noticed that smaller leaflets were arranged in pairs along a central stem. She also saw thin lines (veins) running through each leaflet. Which word best describes what she observed?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. This item tests whether students can apply the chapter's definition of a pattern — a repeating arrangement of shapes — to a fresh natural example.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record repeating patterns on natural objects through careful looking and drawing.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates the student focused on visual appearance generally rather than on the repeating structural arrangement — a surface-level reading of the observation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Shows confusion between texture (how a surface feels) and pattern (a repeating arrangement) — both are surface properties but different ones.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student has not connected the observation to any meaningful category and chose a random visual word.

assessment_items.task: Draw an animal that has a pattern on its body. Then, next to it, draw a piece of pottery — a pot, a plate, or a tile — that uses a similar pattern as its decoration. Below both drawings, write one sentence explaining how the artist might have got the idea for the pot's pattern.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think of an animal with stripes, spots, or repeating shapes on its body. Draw the animal and carefully add the pattern. Now imagine you are the artist: look at the animal's pattern — what shapes does it use? Draw a pot and put a similar pattern on it. Your sentence might begin: 'The artist may have looked at ___ and used its ___ pattern to decorate the pot.'
format_of_output: Drawing of a pot or pottery piece decorated with a similar pattern
One sentence connecting the animal pattern to the artist's inspiration
assessment_items.annotation: The animal and pot patterns need not be identical — credit any clear visual relationship (e.g. zebra stripes on a pot, leopard spots on a plate). The written sentence must make an explicit connection between observing nature and artistic choice. Accept regional art traditions (e.g. Madhubani leaf motifs, Warli animal figures) as equally valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent patterns observed in nature and in human-made objects through drawing, identifying the repeating element.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can identify a repeating element in a natural pattern and deliberately transfer it to a human-made decorative object, then articulate the nature-to-art connection in words.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold walks students from choosing an animal to identifying its repeating unit to transferring it — look for deliberate visual correspondence rather than two unrelated drawings.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: visually recognisable animal, a pot with a pattern that clearly echoes the animal's, a sentence naming both the animal and the pattern element. Weak: animal and pot patterns share no visible relationship, sentence is generic ('artists look at things').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle to draw the animal in detail may draw just the pattern itself (stripes, spots) and label it. Students who excel may create a more complex repeating design.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Two drawings with a connecting sentence
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The paired drawing structure makes the nature-to-art transfer visible and assessable, while the sentence adds a verbal dimension that checks conceptual understanding.

assessment_items.question_text:
Look at these six steps in pot-making, listed below in the wrong order. Rewrite them as a numbered list from 1 to 6 in the correct order.

— Baking the shaped pot in the kiln
— Collecting clay from a wet or muddy place
— Adding patterns and colours to decorate the pot
— Kneading the wet clay until it is smooth and dough-like
— Removing the finished pot from the kiln
— Shaping the clay into a pot on the wheel
expected_elements: 1. Collecting clay from a wet or muddy place
2. Kneading the wet clay until it is smooth and dough-like
3. Shaping the clay into a pot on the wheel
4. Adding patterns and colours to decorate the pot
5. Baking the shaped pot in the kiln
6. Removing the finished pot from the kiln
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for the exact sequence above. The only acceptable variation: decoration (step 4) may be placed after firing (step 5) if a student notes that some pottery traditions paint after firing — accept this with a brief written reason. Do not penalise if the student swaps steps 1 and 2 and provides a rationale.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can sequence the stages of a making process in logical order, justifying each step using cause-and-effect reasoning.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: 1. Collecting clay from a wet or muddy place
2. Kneading the wet clay until it is smooth and dough-like
3. Shaping the clay into a pot on the wheel
4. Adding patterns and colours to decorate the pot
5. Baking the shaped pot in the kiln
6. Removing the finished pot from the kiln

assessment_items.question_text: Rohan noticed that bricks are made from mud, shaped using moulds, and then baked in a kiln — just like pots. Which statement best explains why potters and brick-makers use the same basic process?

options.label: A
options.text: Both potters and brick-makers learned the process from the same person.

options.label: B
options.text: Bricks and pots are the same shape, so they need the same moulds.

options.label: C
options.text: Clay and mud become hard and long-lasting when heat drives out moisture, so both crafts use a kiln.

options.label: D
options.text: Mud is easier to find than stone, so builders prefer to use it for everything.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. This item tests whether students can transfer the material-property reasoning from pottery to a new application (bricks) — a key cross-section link in the chapter.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare two making processes to identify shared steps, and connect the materials used for shelter to the local environment.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a social explanation where a material-property explanation is needed — the student has not connected the shared process to the shared behaviour of clay/mud under heat.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Shows a shape-based confusion: the student focused on the objects' appearance rather than the underlying material transformation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the student partially understood (mud is a local material) but replaced the heat-hardening explanation with an availability argument that does not explain the kiln step.

assessment_items.question_text: A family in a hot and dry part of India builds their house from mud and uses a mixture of cow dung and water to plaster the walls and floor. A visitor says, 'Why don't they just use bricks? Mud houses are old-fashioned.' Do you agree with the visitor? Give at least two reasons to support your answer.
look_for: Disagrees with the visitor (or qualifies agreement) and explains that mud houses suit the local environment.
Provides at least one reason related to the natural properties of mud and cow-dung plaster — e.g. keeps interiors cool, repels insects, requires no factory production.
Provides at least one reason related to local availability and cost — mud is found nearby, no transport needed, affordable for families.
Shows awareness of trade-offs — acknowledges mud houses can be damaged by heavy rain, without concluding they are inferior overall.
Uses evaluative language that goes beyond simple fact-recall — e.g. 'it depends on where you live', 'for this environment it is a good choice'.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept both 'I disagree' and nuanced 'it depends' positions, provided the student supports their position with evidence from the chapter. Do not penalise students from regions where brick is the norm if they acknowledge why mud suits other regions.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can give reasoned explanations for why a traditional building practice is environmentally suited to its context.

competency.competency_text: Identifies the needs of people in different situations – in terms of access to resources, equal opportunities, work distribution, and shelter

Provides at least one reason related to the natural properties of mud and cow-dung plaster — e.g. keeps interiors cool, repels insects, requires no factory production.
Provides at least one reason related to local availability and cost — mud is found nearby, no transport needed, affordable for families.
Shows awareness of trade-offs — acknowledges mud houses can be damaged by heavy rain, without concluding they are inferior overall.
Uses evaluative language that goes beyond simple fact-recall — e.g. 'it depends on where you live', 'for this environment it is a good choice'.

assessment_items.question_text:
The table below shows four types of houses and where they are found.

| House type | Where it is found |
|---|---|
| Tent | Open grasslands or deserts |
| Houseboat | On a river or lake |
| Stone house | Rocky mountain areas |
| Multi-storey building | Large cities |

Which house type would be MOST useful for a family that moves from place to place with their animals?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: C. This item checks whether students can match a shelter need (mobility) to its most suitable type — the core skill of the observation-and-matching activity. The table format mirrors the textbook task.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify different types of shelter from visual observation and match each to the environmental or geographic context it suits.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the student matched 'large' or 'strong' to the idea of many animals, ignoring the mobility requirement — a misconception about what nomadic life needs.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Shows the student associated 'natural material' (stone) with a natural lifestyle, but missed that a stone house cannot be moved.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student connected 'water' to animals needing water, rather than reading 'moves from place to place' as the key criterion.

assessment_items.question_text: Riya and her group made two small walls from dough bricks. In Wall 1 the bricks were stacked in straight columns (joints lined up). In Wall 2 the bricks were staggered (each brick sits across the gap between two bricks below). When they pushed both walls gently, Wall 2 stayed up longer. Explain why the staggered arrangement is sturdier, using what you know about how force travels through a wall.
expected_elements: In the aligned arrangement, the joints (gaps between bricks) line up vertically, so a push travels straight down through the same weak points in every row.
In the staggered arrangement, each brick sits across the joint of the row below, so the force is spread across more bricks instead of passing through the same gap.
Spreading force across more bricks makes it harder for the wall to split apart at one point.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for all three elements. Award partial credit for one or two elements. Accept informal language ('the force spreads out', 'no weak line to break along') as equivalent to technical phrasing.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can carry out a fair comparison test, record what they observe, and use the evidence to explain why one structural arrangement is stronger than another.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: In the aligned arrangement, the joints (gaps between bricks) line up vertically, so a push travels straight down through the same weak points in every row.
In the staggered arrangement, each brick sits across the joint of the row below, so the force is spread across more bricks instead of passing through the same gap.
Spreading force across more bricks makes it harder for the wall to split apart at one point.

assessment_items.task: Choose one safety rule that people follow at a construction site, at home, or at school. Draw a picture showing a person following that rule correctly. Write one sentence below your drawing that explains WHY this rule keeps people safe.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about: What could go wrong if this rule is not followed? Who could be hurt? Your drawing should show what the SAFE action looks like — not the dangerous one. Your sentence should start with the rule and end with the reason: for example, 'Workers wear helmets because falling objects can hurt their heads.'
format_of_output: A pencil or colour-pencil drawing showing the safe behaviour in action
One sentence explaining why the rule keeps people safe
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any safety rule from any of the three settings (construction site, home, school). The drawing must show the safe action (not the hazard alone). The sentence must include a reason, not just restate the rule. Regional safety practices (e.g. wearing a dupatta away from machinery, not playing near a well) are equally valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify safety practices in different settings and explain the reasoning behind each rule.

competency.competency_text: Identifies the needs of people in different situations – in terms of access to resources, equal opportunities, work distribution, and shelter

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can identify a concrete safety behaviour and articulate a cause-effect explanation for why it protects people.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold directs students to show the safe action and to structure their sentence as rule + reason — look for both elements in the output.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a clear scene showing a specific safe action, a sentence that names the hazard being prevented and why the rule addresses it. Weak: a drawing of the hazard without the safe response, a sentence that only restates the rule without a reason.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may write two sentences instead — one describing the rule and one explaining the reason. Students who excel may add a second example.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The combination of a drawn scene and a written reason asks students to demonstrate both recognition of the behaviour and understanding of its purpose.

assessment_items.question_text: Write the steps of pot-making in the correct order. Then explain in one or two sentences what a kiln is and why it is an important part of the process.
expected_elements: Correct sequence of pot-making steps: collect clay → knead/prepare → shape on wheel → decorate → bake in kiln → remove finished pot.
A kiln is a very hot oven used to bake shaped clay objects.
The kiln is important because its heat drives out all moisture and makes the clay permanently hard, so the pot can hold water and last a long time.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for a correct sequence (minor variation in decoration placement is acceptable) plus both elements of the kiln explanation — what it is and what it does. Award partial credit for one element missing.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can write a sequenced account of a making process and explain the purpose of a key step, using their own words.

assessment_items.question_text: A student says: 'Artists just make up designs from their imagination — they don't need to look at nature.' Do you agree or disagree? Use examples from this chapter to support your answer, and explain what you think would be different about art and pottery if there were no patterns in nature.
look_for: Disagrees with the student's claim (or qualifies it) and states that many artists observe natural patterns before creating.
Provides at least one specific example of a natural pattern from the chapter — zebra stripes, leopard spots, leaf arrangements, squirrel stripes — and connects it to artistic decoration.
Explains that pottery and other decorative traditions across India draw on nature's shapes and patterns.
Engages with the 'what if no patterns in nature' question — suggests that art would look different, less varied, or that artists would have fewer sources of inspiration.
Response shows reasoning that moves beyond fact-recall to a personal evaluative position supported by evidence.
assessment_items.annotation: Award higher marks for responses that connect a named natural pattern to a named artistic use AND engage with the hypothetical question. Regional art forms (Madhubani, Warli, Kolam) that use nature motifs are valid and should be credited if mentioned.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect observation of natural patterns to artistic inspiration, and discuss what the world might look like if patterns were absent.

assessment_items.task: Draw and colour three different kinds of houses. Under each drawing, write the name of the house and one sentence that explains why that house suits the place or environment where it is found.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about where each house is built — is it near water? In the mountains? In a busy city? In a hot, dry area? Think about what the house is made of and why that material makes sense for that place. Your sentence might start: 'This house is good for ___ because ___.'
format_of_output: Three drawings of different house types, each coloured
The name of each house type written beneath its drawing
One sentence per house explaining why it suits its environment
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any three distinct house types from the chapter or from the student's own knowledge (mud house, tent, houseboat, stone house, multi-storey building, thatched roof house, stilt house, etc.). The sentence must link the house to its environment, not just describe the material. Regional variation note: houses specific to the student's region — e.g. a pucca house in the plains, a bamboo house in the northeast — are equally valid and should be credited.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent diverse shelter types through drawing and label each with its material and the environmental reason for its design.

competency.competency_text: Identifies the needs of people in different situations – in terms of access to resources, equal opportunities, work distribution, and shelter

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can visually represent diverse shelter types and articulate the environment-to-design reasoning for each — not just name or copy the house.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides students to think about location and material before drawing — look for drawings that reflect a deliberate choice (a tent in open land, a houseboat on water) rather than three generic box-houses.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: three visually distinct houses, each with a name and a sentence that explicitly connects material or design to environment. Weak: three similar-looking houses, names without sentences, or sentences that only state the material without the environment reason.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle to draw in detail may sketch outlines and focus energy on the written sentence. Students who excel may add people, landscape features, or labels of the building material.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Three labelled drawings with explanatory sentences
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The combination of drawing and sentence requires both visual recognition and verbal reasoning, mirroring the dual demand of the textbook task.

assessment_items.question_text: Mita is curious about how the eraser she uses every day is made. She knows it is soft and bouncy and can rub out pencil marks. List two things she could do to find out how erasers are made, and write one step in the making process that you think is involved — based on what you have learned about how natural materials are changed to make useful objects.
expected_elements: Two inquiry actions — e.g. ask an elder or family member who might know; look it up in a book or video; ask a shopkeeper; observe the material and reason from its properties.

One plausible step in the making of an eraser — e.g. rubber is collected from a rubber tree (tapped as liquid latex), the latex is shaped into a block using a mould, it may be heated or treated to make it firm. (Accept any reasonable step; do not require technical accuracy.)
The proposed step should reflect the broader principle from the chapter — a natural material is collected, processed, and shaped — even if the specific detail is uncertain.
assessment_items.annotation: The key skill being assessed is inquiry thinking and transfer of the natural-material-transformation principle, not technical knowledge of rubber manufacturing. Award full credit for two sensible inquiry strategies and one step that applies the chapter's transformation logic. Award partial credit for one inquiry strategy or one step alone.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace the material origins of an everyday object and describe the sequence of steps by which a natural material is transformed into it.

assessment_items.question_text: Through this chapter you have explored clay pots, patterns in nature, bricks, mud houses, and everyday objects like pencils and erasers. Choose any two of these topics and explain how human making is connected to the natural world. Use at least one example from each topic you choose.
look_for: Selects two topics from the chapter and provides at least one specific example from each.
For each topic, makes an explicit connection between a natural material or natural pattern and a human-made product or practice.
Shows understanding that the connection runs in both directions — nature provides the material or inspiration, and humans transform or use it.
Demonstrates cross-chapter reasoning — the response is not simply a retelling of one section but draws threads between sections.
Uses evaluative or reflective language — e.g. 'this shows that people have always depended on nature', 'without the natural world, these things could not be made'.
assessment_items.annotation: This synthesis item is the chapter's most open-ended assessment. Credit any two topics from the chapter. Award higher marks for responses that move beyond description to reflection on the nature-human connection as a broader idea. Accept regional examples (local pottery traditions, bamboo craft, palm-leaf objects) alongside textbook examples.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect ideas across a chapter — natural materials, craft traditions, patterns in nature, and diverse shelters — into a coherent account of how human making is shaped by the natural world.
